title: GS Retail Teams Up with aT to Expand Traditional Liquor Sales and Support Local Breweries - 아시아경제

GS Retail Teams Up with aT to Expand Traditional Liquor Sales and Support Local Breweries GS Retail said on October 13 that it had signed a business agreement with the Korea Agro-Fisheries & Food Trade Corporation (aT) to promote consumption of traditional alcoholic beverages and expand sales channels for local breweries. Senior officials from both sides, including GS Retail O4O Division Head Jeon Jinhyeok and aT Export Foods Director Jeon Gichan, attended the signing ceremony. The two sides agreed to link GS Retail's online and offline distribution networks with aT's traditional liquor promotion programs to increase sales and promotion of high-quality traditional alcoholic beverages. GS Retail's Jeon Jinhyeok, head of the O4O Division (left), and aT Export Foods Director Jeon Gichan (right) signed a memorandum of understanding to boost traditional liquor consumption and expand sales channels for local breweries. GS Retail First, GS Retail will feature traditional alcoholic beverages recommended by aT and award-winning entries from the Korean Traditional Liquor Awards through its Wine25Plus liquor smart-ordering service. Customers can order products online and pick them up at a nearby GS25 or GS The Fresh store. Depending on sales performance, the companies plan to expand sales to offline stores. In October, GS Retail will operate a dedicated section for traditional alcoholic beverages on Wine25Plus, and in November it will open a "Brewery Visits" section. The companies will also organize joint promotions at the end of the year, including traditional liquor home party packages. They will also launch a local brand development campaign introducing traditional alcoholic beverages made by local breweries using locally grown agricultural products. "We expect this agreement to help introduce high-quality traditional alcoholic beverages and local breweries to customers, while expanding opportunities for consumers to discover and purchase traditional alcoholic beverages more conveniently," said Jeon Jinhyeok, head of GS Retail's O4O Division. "We will continue to strengthen our mutually beneficial partnerships with local breweries by leveraging GS Retail's online and offline distribution networks, and enhance our platform's competitiveness by presenting distinctive traditional alcoholic beverage products and content." © The Asia Business Daily. title: The Cheap Adventure Bike That Makes A Used BMW GS Look Like A Financial Mistake - HotCars
content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update The BMW GS has evolved into something of an institution within the adventure community. Even though it is one of the most expensive ADVs on the used market, especially one with a few BMW-approved accessories, it is still incredibly popular. For most adventure enthusiasts, it has become the default choice, but we feel that there are a selection of more affordable options that all do a better job. Price is also only part of the problem. The GS weighs well over 500 pounds, and has a relatively tall seat height. It is easy to ride around this on the street, but it becomes far more challenging to deal with once you have your first spill off-road. Lifting one of these bikes is pretty easy on a flat surface, but very few trails offer that level of convenience. While these bigger adventure bikes are great tourers, they can sap one’s confidence off-road. For most riders, the whole point of owning an ADV is to go exploring off-road, and everything else is secondary. The solution comes in the form of a lighter middleweight, which offers a better balance between off-road competence and touring comfort. Today, we have a wide selection of impressive middleweights to choose from, with pretty much every major manufacturer producing one. It is fair to say that the Tenere 700 gave the middleweight market the shot in the arm it needed. Up until it made its global debut all the way back in 2019, most middleweight options were pretty heavy, relatively slow, and generally failed to capture the imagination. The Tenere, on the other hand, was light, fast, and promised us Dakar-level capability with the pre-production T7. Naturally, its final version was a little watered down, but not quite as much as people speculated. It was still a hard-edged off-road oriented machine. Customers in the US had to wait another two years, but it was worth the wait, and Yamaha actually struggled to keep up with demand for a time. Five years later, the competition has increased, and the price of the Tenere has gone up, yet it still offers sensational value to the right buyer. Most middleweight adventure bikes make use of reliable, modern twins, but out of all the 270 degree parallel-twins currently on the market, the CP2 is inarguably the most reliable. In fact, it is one of the most reliable motorcycle engines ever produced, at least when it comes to larger displacement bikes. When it comes to motorcycles that are used for travel, the kind of peace of mind is a genuine point of difference. Like most modern crossplane twins, it does a great job of emulating a V-twin. Even though 73 horsepower may not seem much when compared to its direct rivals, the way it delivers its power makes it a fun bike to ride out in the real world. Pretty much all of its torque is available from around 2,000 RPM, so the roll-on power is exceptional, and it doesn’t have all that much weight to lug around in the first place. The Tenere was initially a back-to-basics offering, and was intentionally sparsely equipped in an effort to keep the price down. While the rugged simplicity of the original was appealing to some, many adventure enthusiasts lamented its glaring lack of features when compared to its most direct rivals. Yamaha responded in kind by gradually updating the platform, and now, five years after it was first released in the US, it is very much the finished article. A ride-by-wire throttle was introduced, and this enables the two ride modes. It also gets ABS and traction control, which are both switchable. The original bike had a robust LCD dash, but the latest bike gets a big TFT dash with smartphone connectivity. In our opinion, these updates are all there simply to keep up with what the competition has on offer, but the most meaningful update came in the form of an improved rear shock. It was easily the biggest gripe with the original bike, and the fact that Yamaha listened to customer feedback says a lot about the brand. Unfortunately, every motorcycle is a compromise. With the extra effort Yamaha put into making the Tenere more competent off-road, you do lose some level of touring comfort. Out of all the middleweight bikes currently competing in this space, the Yamaha might actually have the worst seat. It is essentially a dirt-bike seat which works great while you are standing up off-road, but after around an hour on the highway, pretty much everything below your waist will lose feeling. For riders who will be using their ADV for long distance travel, this can be a deal-breaker, but there are aftermarket solutions available. The other factor counting against the Tenere is how much the competition has improved over the years. It lacks a certain level of sophistication, and certainly feels more like a budget offering than a late model GS would. But, if you want a more sophisticated version of the Tenere, Yamaha will gladly point you in the direction of the new World Raid edition which has a host of additional features, including an IMU-backed electronics suite, uprated KYB suspension, and a long-range fuel tank. Its tasteful Intensity White livery also gives the bike a premium feel. It is well worth considering, especially when you take into account the fact that its base price of $13k is still $3k less than what you would have to fork out for a five-year-old BMW. Objectively speaking, that is sensational value. But, the base model still has its place, and honestly makes that used GS look like a pretty poor financial decision when you look at the price difference. We want to hear from you. title: GS Caltex Wins Two Awards at London International Awards; Campaign Promoting Low-Carbon Technology Praised - 아시아경제
content:
GS Caltex Wins Two Awards at London International Awards; Campaign Promoting Low-Carbon Technology Praised GS Caltex said on the 13th that its “CCU-S (Kkusseu)” campaign, launched to promote its new low-carbon businesses, won two awards at the 2026 London International Awards. Award-winning creative image for GS Caltex at the London International Awards. GS Caltex GS Caltex won Silver in the “Creative Public Relations” category and Bronze in the “Creative Strategy” category. The London International Awards, established in 1986, is an international advertising festival that evaluates entries in various fields, including advertising, public relations, strategy, and design. The award-winning “Kkusseu” campaign was designed to explain carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technology to the public in an accessible way. In particular, it turned the process of capturing gas and using it to grow plants into a game through the “CCUS KIT,” an interactive educational tool that compares carbon gas to “farts,” a subject familiar to children. GS Caltex ran the campaign in collaboration with advertising agency Ideot. It produced content explaining the principles of CCUS with science creator Orbit, and this year also provided carbon-reduction education to about 500 students at seven elementary schools in the Yeosu area. Before this award, the Kkusseu campaign was shortlisted in four categories at the New York Festivals in June and won a Crystal Award in the Strategy category at the Busan International Marketing Advertising Festival in August. GS Caltex is pursuing new low-carbon businesses, including CCUS, carbon-free steam, biofuels, and waste-plastic recycling. A GS Caltex representative said, “This award recognizes our ability to communicate complex and specialized low-carbon technologies in a way that the public can understand and relate to.” The representative added, “We will continue communicating so that customers and society can easily understand the value of our businesses and technologies.” © The Asia Business Daily. In 1997, the Glastron GS 209 arrived from the United States—a fast, easily trailerable boat with two berths and a distinctly American style. Excerpted from *Barche a Motore*, 1995, No. 7, August, pp. 82–89. Fiart SX5 (17m): the new cruiser with plenty of open space on the water The boats built by the American shipyard Glastron—imported into Italy by Promonautica in 18 different models—boast seagoing qualities and speed performance that are well concealed by their attractive, unassuming appearance. Available in multiple versions, they offer a good balance between livability and cruising comfort. The generous beam compared to the overall length of the vessel has allowed the Glastron shipyard to create a spacious cabin and a deck for the GS 209 that can comfortably accommodate the crew. Access to the non-slip foredeck is via a central opening in the windshield. The swim platform is structural, molded into the mold. The waterlines are excellent, keeping the hull on course without cavitation even during the tightest turns. New Verga Sestante 6.8 (6.8 m): the boat with a sea wolf VIDEO and PRICE To prevent osmosis, the Glastron shipyard uses a fiberglass fabric called BiTex for the lamination process. This fabric features a dense multidirectional weave that absorbs just the right amount of resin, resulting in a product that is both elastic and resistant, lighter in weight and more precise in its lamination. To reinforce the underwater hull, instead of wood embedded in fiberglass—which can deteriorate over time—a special vitrifiable foam is used to make the structure more rigid in the areas most subject to stress, while significantly reducing weight. The resulting structure is covered by a five-year structural warranty and a two-year warranty for the other components built by the shipyard. Starting from the swim platform (1.86 x 0.32 m), equipped with a ladder for reboarding after swimming and an efficient stainless steel handrail, you have direct access to the aft sundeck (1.85 x 0.95 m) built above the engine compartment, which is unfortunately only partially raised by two gas pistons. The engine compartment is very spacious and can accommodate the awning and the ribs inside. Moving toward the bow, you’ll find the multi-seat transverse sofa and, even further forward, the two swiveling, bucket-style seats for the pilot and co-pilot. The helm station is well-equipped and features a comfortable footrest that conceals a spacious storage compartment. In the floor, there is an additional storage locker—unfortunately also carpeted—though it is equipped with a drain. The bow is well protected by the high gunwale. The Glastron GS 209 ‘s interior is accessed through a folding door. The furnishings include an armchair and two V-shaped bunks that convert to a double bed. A chemical toilet is located under the bed. The Volvo Penta 4.3 GL SX sterndrive is a four-stroke, six-cylinder V-engine petrol engine that develops 205 hp and is seawater-cooled, with a displacement of 4300 cc. The transmission is a single-propeller SX. The main quality of this fast hull is its directionality: at full revs it is possible to make turns with a very tight radius without cavitation; the hull seems to run on rails. title: Granny G’s Celebrates MN’s Women Athletes With Hot Dogs Fried in Butter - Racket
content: At Minneapolis's North Star Deli, the menu and the decor are guided by a love of old-school Minnesota hockey. You’ve got your Herb Brooks Focaccia, your Gump’s Green Wrap, your Dino Italian Sub. Every surface is covered in memorabilia—Slap Shot figurines and Jesse Ventura action figures accompany vintage North Stars gear, a nod to the stuff chef Pedro Wolcott fell in love with, improbably, when he was introduced to Minnesota and hockey while watching The Mighty Ducks as a kid growing up in Panama. But one thing about old-time hockey? Not a lot of women in the mix. And Wolcott, looking around his Kingfield sandwich shop, thought it might be fun to do something with more of a femme focus. He has a daughter, after all—shouldn’t she see herself represented in sports and in her dad’s restaurant? “The women do so great, I don’t know why we never give them their due,” Wolcott says. (He’s right; nobody say anything about how the Lynx season ended.) This was the inspiration behind Granny G’s, Wolcott’s new hot dog trailer, where the dogs have names like The Lynx Glizzy (bacon bits, sauerkraut, caramelized onion) and Granny’s Kimchi Kick (gochujang spicy mayo, kimchi slaw, fried jalapeños, and wontons). Portraits of Olivia Miles by local artist Adam Johnson (of Naz Reid yard sign fame) greet you as you walk up to the truck, and the inside of the space, though tiny, is packed with more stuff: hockey sticks, pennants, grinning StudBudz. “This is like a typical food trailer in New Orleans,” Wolcott says, likening the decorations to those in over-the-top Big Easy spots like Turkey and the Wolf. “If I could have a TV in here with VHS playing, I would.” The focus is on Minnesota’s women’s sports teams, but New Orleans isn’t the only other city from which Wolcott draws inspiration. “These are upstate New York-style hot dogs, so we fry them in butter,” he says. He’s a longtime fan of Walter's Hot Dog Stand, which serves split-grilled dogs like these in its National Register of Historic Places-designated spot in Mamaroneck, New York. As for the chili? Wolcott has always loved the chili from Tommy’s in Los Angeles, where they slap the stuff on everything from burgers to breakfast burritos. But far-flung as Granny’s meaty muses may be, the ingredients are very local. Wolcott gets his hot dogs and sausages from Kramarczuk's in Northeast, and the “meats” for the vegan versions come from the Herbivorous Butcher. All of the buns are baked by Turtle Bread on Chicago Avenue. I don’t know that I’ve ever had a hot dog fried in butter before, but this method—dogs are butterflied, then fried—gives you a really snappy sausage, as rich and decadent as you’d expect a hot dog fried in butter to be. I’ve also never been to Tommy’s in L.A., but I love the chili that tops Granny’s Chili Cheese Dog ($9.99). Incredibly beefy and meaty, its richness is offset a bit by pickles, tomato, and sliced white onion, though I will caution you to grab a fistful of napkins if you order it, as this was one messy hot dog. Argentinian sausage is the buttery, splayed beef product that serves as the base of the Frost Power Play ($11.99), which is dressed with a wonderfully herbaceous chimichurri mayo and topped with crunchy potato strings. It’s a successful combination—perhaps more successful than the Frost power play was itself in the postseason this year. We’ll get the Walter Cup back in 2027, ladies. And lest your eyes pop at the price of a hot dog here (what are we, literally at a Frost game?), I’ll add that these churched-up little doggies are a whole-ass meal. I didn’t have my measuring tape handy, but I think they were about a foot long, and Granny G’s doesn’t skimp on the toppings. (Again: napkins!) Wolcott says he’s working to find a permanent spot in south Minneapolis for Granny G’s, but for now, he’s content periodically popping up at local businesses or just setting up in front of his Kingfield sandwich shop. Follow along on Instagram @grannyglizzys for info on upcoming pop-ups, including events later this month at Silverbird Coffee and Time Bomb Vintage. title: Korea Expressway Corporation upsets GS Caltex 3-1 in Yeosu cup opener - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) Highpass beat the V-league defending champion GS Caltex KIXX to open their first game with a victory. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) defeated GS Caltex 3-1 (25-18, 25-18, 20-25, 25-19) in the first match of group B of the 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup professional volleyball tournament held Dec. 12 at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu, Gwangju, Jeonnam. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC)'s marquee attacker Moma led the team to victory with 25 points (attack success rate 42.7%). Kang Sohwi (14 points) and Mami (10 points) also contributed double-digit scoring. For GS Caltex, Silva scored 22 points and Choi Ga-eun (12 points) and Thanacha (10 points) joined the attack but could not prevent the team's loss. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) and GS Caltex met in last season's V-league championship finals. At that time GS Caltex won all three games 3-0 to claim the title. Although it was only a cup tournament group stage match, Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) succeeded in avenging that loss against GS Caltex. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) pressed GS Caltex from the first set. The score gap widened from midset and the first set ended without incident. The second set was the same. Early on GS Caltex led and a fierce battle continued, but Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) began to widen the margin from the late part of the set. In an instant the gap grew and Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) took a 2-0 lead in the set score. GS Caltex launched a comeback in the third set. From the start of the set they launched a barrage and seized the momentum early. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) did not force a reckless chase, and GS Caltex succeeded in taking back one set. Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) reorganized in the fourth set. GS Caltex led until 10-6, but Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) narrowed the gap in an instant with three consecutive points and eventually tied it at 14-14. GS Caltex moved ahead again at 17-14, but in a long rally Korea Expressway Corporation (KEC) seized an opportunity from GS Caltex's attacking error and reversed the set with six consecutive points, ultimately taking the victory. title: Korea Expressway Hi-Pass Avenges Defeat, Beats GS Caltex 3-1 - 조선일보
content: Star Attacker Moma Scores 25 Points in Yeosu Cup Victory [OSEN=Gil JoonYoung, reporter] Korea Expressway Corporation Hi-Pass defeated the ‘V-League defending champion’ GS Caltex KIXX to secure a victory in their first match. Korea Expressway Corporation won 3-1 (25-18, 25-18, 20-25, 25-19) against GS Caltex in their first Group B match of the ‘2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament’ held at the Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu City, Jeonnam-Gwangju on October 12. Korea Expressway Corporation’s star attacker Moma led the team to victory with 25 points, 42.7% attack success rate. Kang SoHwi (14 points) and Mami (10 points) also contributed with double-digit scores. GS Caltex’s Silva recorded 22 points, while Choi Ga-eun (12 points) and Tanacha (10 points) joined the attack, but they failed to prevent the team’s defeat. Korea Expressway Corporation and GS Caltex faced each other in the V-League Championship Finals last season. At that time, GS Caltex won three consecutive matches to claim the title. Although this was a group-stage match in the cup tournament, Korea Expressway Corporation successfully avenged their previous loss against GS Caltex. Korea Expressway Corporation pressured GS Caltex from the first set. The score gap widened from the middle of the set, and the first set ended without any variables. The second set followed a similar pattern. GS Caltex took an early lead, leading to a fierce battle, but Korea Expressway Corporation gradually expanded the gap from the latter half of the set. They secured a 2-0 lead in set score. GS Caltex launched a counterattack in the third set. They seized the initiative early in the set with a series of aggressive plays. Korea Expressway Corporation did not pursue recklessly, and GS Caltex successfully narrowed the gap by winning one set. Korea Expressway Corporation reorganized their formation in the fourth set. GS Caltex led 10-6, but Korea Expressway Corporation narrowed the gap with three consecutive points and eventually tied at 14-14. GS Caltex pulled ahead again at 17-14, but Korea Expressway Corporation capitalized on GS Caltex’s attack error in a long rally, scoring six consecutive points to overturn the set and secure the final victory.

title: Korea Expressway Corporation Defeats GS Caltex 3-1 - 조선일보
content: Moma's 25 points lead team to first tournament victory in Yeosu Cup [Yeosu=Sports Chosun Na Yurim Reporter] Moma smiled. The Korea Expressway Corporation volleyball team defeated GS Caltex with a set score of 3-1 (25-18, 25-18, 20-25, 25-19) in a group stage match at the 2026 Yeosu·NH Nonghyup Cup Professional Volleyball Tournament held at Jinnam Gymnasium in Yeosu on the 12th. Korea Expressway Corporation, which secured their first victory in the tournament, was led to victory by Moma’s 25 points, Kang So-hwi’s 13 points, and Mami’s 10 points each. This match was the GS Caltex debut of Thai Asian quota player Thanacha. Thanacha, who played for Korea Expressway Corporation last season, signed with GS Caltex ahead of this season. Coincidentally, Thanacha’s first official match against her former team was also against Korea Expressway Corporation, with whom she had developed close relationships. Ahead of the match, acting head coach Kim Young-rae expressed mixed feelings, saying, “It felt strange. She was a player who often joked around, and (we grew close). It’s natural for players to want to experience different teams, and we respect that. Although we were disappointed, we believe the team has become more solid defensively with the addition of Mami.” GS Caltex head coach Lee Young-taek, who is also very familiar with the opponent, expressed optimism, saying, “I’m worried about how Thanacha will perform against Korea Expressway Corporation. However, she worked hard, and if she performs well in the early stages, I believe she can do well.” As expected, the match turned into a showdown between the two teams’ key aces: GS Caltex’s Silva and Korea Expressway Corporation’s Moma. GS Caltex took an early lead in the first set with Silva’s powerful spikes, but Korea Expressway Corporation countered with Moma’s serves. While GS Caltex struggled with unforced errors, Korea Expressway Corporation maintained a 50% attack success rate, scoring points whenever needed. Notably, Moma and Mami combined for 12 points in the first set, which proved decisive. Korea Expressway Corporation comfortably won the first set. The second set was closely contested, with the score seesawing back and forth. However, at 14-14, Korea Expressway Corporation pulled ahead by three points (17-14) with Moma’s back-row attack success, Kim Da-eun’s ace serve, and a blocking point by Moma against Thanacha’s attack after a long rally. GS Caltex turned to Silva to resolve the situation, but Moma blocked Silva’s attempts with blocking assists, leading to a fiery battle. Moma then exploded with points, contributing to the team’s 20th point. When Silva was blocked, GS Caltex began to falter. Korea Expressway Corporation capitalized on GS Caltex’s shaky reception and comfortably took the second set. GS Caltex took the third set. Thanacha, who had been quiet, began to shine. Although Kim Mi-yeon and Silva extended the lead with their points, Korea Expressway Corporation mounted a strong comeback with points from Kang So-hwi and Mami. In the middle of the third set, Park Jeong-ah, who was substituted in for the first time, changed the momentum with open attacks and blocks. However, GS Caltex, led by Silva, secured their first set win as Thanacha’s consecutive serving points in the closing stages proved decisive. The fourth set was also a close battle. GS Caltex led 10-6, but Korea Expressway Corporation capitalized on scoring opportunities to close the gap to one point. The intense battle continued, with GS Caltex pulling ahead and Korea Expressway Corporation chasing closely. Then, Mami’s serve achieved five consecutive points, allowing Korea Expressway Corporation to reverse the deficit instantly. Trailing 14-17, Korea Expressway Corporation scored six straight points to take a 20-17 lead. GS Caltex, drained of energy, completely collapsed, and Korea Expressway Corporation secured a decisive victory.

title: Five Big Banks, Two Days, One Question: Can Record Trading Offset the Pressure From Rising Yields? - The Globe and Mail

They report after a demanding stretch for bank shares: over the past month the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index has fallen 9.7% while the S&P 500 gained about 1.5%, according to The Motley Fool, as the 10-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2002 and the Federal Reserve delivered its first rate increase in more than three years. The 10-year Treasury yield closed Friday at 5.24% after recently reaching its highest level since 2002, and the University of Michigan’s preliminary October survey showed consumers expect inflation of 4.7% over the next year. Rising yields reduce the market value of fixed-rate securities on bank balance sheets and can push depositors toward higher-yielding alternatives, even as they allow banks to earn more on new loans. Against that backdrop, the second quarter set a high bar. All five banks reported higher earnings than a year earlier. JPMorgan said revenue in each of its lines of business hit a new record, and Morgan Stanley reported record net revenues and record equity trading revenues. title: Asus ROG Strix GS-BE7200 review: A lightning-fast router that’s not just great for gamers - Expert Reviews
content: To help us provide you with free impartial advice, we may earn a commission if you buy through links on our site. Learn more The Asus ROG (“Republic of Gamers”) brand is usually found on high-end enthusiast gear, but the ROG Strix GS-BE7200 is very reasonably priced for a Wi-Fi 7 router. And it comes with a strong specification, combining excellent wireless performance with multi-gigabit wired networking and a full complement of game-optimising tools, plus all the regular management features we expect from an Asus router. This makes it an easy recommendation, not just for gamers seeking an affordable network upgrade but for anyone who wants a fast, versatile router – as long as you can live with its rather over-designed image. The ROG Strix GS-BE7200 is a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router, meaning it works on the 2.4GHz and 5GHz radio bands with no support for the newer 6GHz frequency range. That’s a formula we’ve seen many times before, but the BE7200 features some unexpected upgrades. For a start, the 2.4GHz radio is twice as fast as most rivals, with a top connection speed of 1.4Gbits/sec. And things get even more interesting on the 5GHz band. The router claims a maximum speed of 5.8Gbits/sec on this band, corresponding to the familiar 4×4 MIMO standard, but internally it’s built with not four but five physical radio chains. This allows for greater antenna coverage and diversity, enabling a faster, more reliable connection: Asus claims the extra transmitter can improve throughput by up to 15% at long distances. Wired networking is well catered for by a 2.5GbE internet port and a full complement of four 2.5GbE LAN connectors. The only thing that’s notably absent is a USB socket; this isn’t a deal-breaker, but it would have been nice to know you could plug in an external SSD or a 5G dongle should the need arise. Incidentally, don’t get this router mixed up with the ROG Strix GS-BE7200X. Despite the similar model numbers, the two units are quite different. The BE7200X includes a USB port but has fewer multi-gigabit Ethernet connectors, and lacks the fifth radio chain. At £135, the ROG Strix GS-BE7200 costs exactly the same as Asus’ other current gaming router, the TUF Gaming BE9400. However, the two models have little in common: the TUF Gaming router boasts 6GHz Wi-Fi and USB connectivity, but slower top speeds and fewer dedicated gaming features. You pays your money and takes your choice. If you’re not specifically looking for a gaming router you might consider one of TP-Link’s rival models, particularly the TP-Link Archer BE400 and TP-Link Archer BE550. The former focuses on 5GHz performance while the latter offers a combination of 5GHz and 6GHz networking; prices are, however, a bit higher than Asus’ offerings, at £160 apiece. If you wanted something a bit cheaper, the Asus ProArt PRT-BE5000 might look like a tempting option, offering an elegant upright design for £10 less than the Strix – but note that it has a slower Wi-Fi radio and only one multi-gigabit LAN port. Another tower-style option is the Netgear Nighthawk RS200, but that’s currently selling for a full £200, making it a bad deal at today’s prices. Needless to say, there are plenty of cheaper Wi-Fi 7 routers, our favourite being the TP-Link Archer BE3600. This isn’t as fast as the other routers we’ve mentioned – it’s equipped with 2.9Gbits/sec Wi-Fi rather than the full 5.8Gbits/sec, but it’s perfectly good for a typical home or even a small office. The ROG Strix GS-BE7200 doesn’t look like any router I’ve ever seen before. Rather than trying to describe the casing, I’ll point you towards my photos and let you draw your own conclusions. Personally, if this were my home router, I’d be inclined to hide it away as far as possible, but you may feel differently. You can even make it look more conspicuous if you want, as the squinty Republic of Gamers logo on the front panel is backed with RGB LEDs that can glow, pulse and breathe in a colour of your choice when the router’s powered on. Or you can turn them off for a slightly more serious image. While the exterior of the router may be unique, the web management interface offers mostly the same layout and features as a regular Asus router. That means all the usual home network management functions are at your fingertips, including subscription-free security checks and parental controls, basic ad-blocking, inbound and outbound VPN support and separate SSIDs for guests, kids and IoT devices. The GS-BE7200 also includes an upgraded QoS feature called adaptive QoE, which includes an “AI balance” mode that’s not found on other Asus routers we’ve recently tested. This continually monitors network activity and dynamically adjusts packet priorities to optimise performance for whatever’s going on at that moment. It’s hard to say whether this really helps with anything, but you can always experiment with it and fall back to traditional rule-based QoS if you prefer. Game-specific features include live meters on the dashboard tracking your internet ping times, and the Game Radar map that shows real-time server status for a handful of popular online games, including Diablo 3 and World of Warcraft, helping you pick the best one to connect to. The Game Boost tools let you prioritise specific clients and mobile devices, while OpenNAT provides preconfigured port forwarding rules for a large library of popular games, so you can get each one working with a few clicks. I have just a few minor complaints about the Asus system software. As ever, the web portal is a maze of tabs and panes, and it often took me a few goes to find the right route to the setting I was looking for. On this particular router it also seems a bit more sluggish to open than usual, probably due to the active gaming widgets embedded on the landing page. You might prefer to use the standard Asus Router smartphone app, which lets you control all the standard features, add port-forwarding rules and control the RGB LEDs, but doesn’t offer the live ping monitoring and Game Radar features. I set up the ROG Strix GS-BE7200 in the upstairs study of my own home, installed the latest firmware and connected an Asustor Drivestor 4 Pro NAS appliance to one of its 2.5GbE sockets. To compare performance with rival routers, I then connected to the 5GHz wireless network from my standard test laptop – a Dell Inspiron equipped with an Intel BE200 Wi-Fi 7 card – and went around my home copying files to and from the NAS, measuring upload and download speeds in different rooms. With its fast 5GHz Wi-Fi hardware and that extra transmitter chain to boost signal quality, the ROG Strix GS-BE7200 performs brilliantly. Here’s how it stacked up in my tests: I’d love to say that the ROG Strix’s download speeds bested every other router in every location; technically that’s not quite true, as the TP-Link Archer BE400 pipped it at close range by the slimmest margin. Overall, though, the Asus ROG Stix GS-BE7200 was unquestionably the champion of the group, consistently delivering first-class performance no matter where I wandered. Indeed, its advantage over other routers was much greater than the advertised 15%. I assume this is down to the router being better able to maintain multi-stream connections that multiply the effective throughput. For once, I actually believe that a router could satisfactorily cover the area claimed by the manufacturer (255 square metres, since you ask). I don’t normally test performance on the 2.4GHz band, as this is typically used by smart home-type devices that have no particular need for speed. But since the ROG Strix GS-BE7200’s 2.4GHz radio is twice as fast as most rivals, I found myself wondering whether it might be good enough for low-priority client devices. Repeating my tests on the 2.4GHz band, I saw a very respectable download speed of 27.4MB/sec in the study, tapering down to 10.7MB/sec in the dining room at the opposite end of my home. While that’s clearly a lot slower than the 5GHz band, it’s fast enough that you could comfortably run smartphones, streaming sticks and security cameras over the 2.4GHz network, and preserve your super-fast 5GHz bandwidth for devices that really benefit from a top-speed connection. Who needs a separate 6GHz radio anyway? The Asus ROG Strix GS-BE7200 is a very impressive router. Based on my real-world tests, I can say its Wi-Fi performance and range are in a different class to any of its rivals’, yet amazingly it’s actually cheaper than most of them. Is it a perfect product? No – in my view it looks stupid, and while the software is powerful, I can’t really call it user-friendly. I also prefer my routers to have a USB port, just for contingencies. But I’m not going to reject a router on looks alone, and hopefully you’ll only need to grapple with the settings once in a blue moon, whereas fast, long-range connectivity is something you’ll appreciate every day. In fact, when shopping for a new Wi-Fi 7 router I’d say the Asus ROG Strix GS-BE7200 should be your default number one choice. It’s fast, affordable and – whether you care about its gaming features or not – fully equipped to run any sort of home network. Just maybe consider tucking it away out of sight when visitors come to call. title: GS Engineering & Construction holds 'Gran Partners Fiesta 2026' with partner firms - 헤럴드경제
content: CEO Heo Yun-hong, executives and over 80 partner firm heads attend Discussions center on physical AI adoption and robot use at construction sites GS Engineering & Construction held its annual partnership event, Gran Partners Fiesta 2026, on Monday at the Grand InterContinental Seoul Parnas in Samseong-dong, Seoul, bringing together CEO Heo Yun-hong, company executives and representatives from more than 80 partner firms. Gran Partners Fiesta is GS Engineering & Construction's flagship partnership event, held continuously for more than 20 years since 2004. It was established to create a space where the company and its partners could grow together and communicate on equal footing. This year's event centered on ways to apply advanced technologies — including physical AI — to construction sites, and on directions for strengthening the industry's long-term competitiveness. Expert lectures were delivered alongside presentations on physical AI technologies already deployed or planned for GS Engineering & Construction sites, and attendees freely exchanged views on expanding robot use at construction sites. Heo stressed the importance of safety at the event and said, "The growth of our partner companies is the growth of GS Engineering & Construction." He added that the company would "expand practical support for partners and continue pursuing mutual growth and co-development based on principled management and open communication." He also said the company would "actively introduce advanced technologies, including physical AI, to build safer and more competitive job sites, and lead the future of the construction industry together with our partners." GS Engineering & Construction operates the "Great Partnership Package" to establish fair trade practices and promote co-development with its partners. The program runs a range of practical support initiatives built around four pillars: fair trade order, financial support, competitiveness enhancement and horizontal communication. Safety is treated as the top priority, with measures including advance payment of industrial safety and health management costs and financial support for dedicated safety managers at high-risk work types. Since 2021, the company has also operated a competitive bidding system to help partners secure adequate profit margins and maintain management stability. To broaden financial support, GS Engineering & Construction runs an annual interest-free management support fund of 15 billion won ($11.2 million) and a 30 billion won co-growth fund. It also draws on a 4 billion won partnership fund to support small and midsize partners across technology and research and development, productivity improvement, and workforce training. Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted operating profit of 232.4 billion won in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.

title: A Valles Caldera ride proves better with company - Albuquerque Journal
content: Support local news. Please select your privacy preferences to continue. A New Mexico adventure motorcyclist joins GS Riders of New Mexico for a scenic group ride I stumbled upon a paradox when I first got into adventure motorcycle riding. I was drawn to the allure of setting out on the open road, just me and my bike, to explore the byways and dirt roads that crisscross vast swaths of our beautiful country. I soon discovered that for reasons of safety and enjoyment, however, this is a hobby best shared with other riders. I bought my 2012 Yamaha Super Tenere — a 1,200 c.c. motorcycle suspended in such a way as to make long stretches of highway and bumpy dirt roads equally manageable — back in spring of 2020. Originally, I was fixated on a BMW model of similar capabilities but for a much higher price tag. I had even sent a few thousand dollars of earnest money to the friend from whom I was to purchase the Beemer when a small hiccup bubbled up. A pandemic, to be precise. My friend kindly refunded me the money. In that moment none of us was very confident of what our financial futures would look like. I cut my budget in half and went shopping for something more affordable. Some people took solace in a new pet to cope with COVID, others binge-watched television or took up cooking. I rode a motorcycle. Six years later, I’m still deeply in love with this big blue bike. I was living in Vermont when I acquired my COVID cure but returned to New Mexico in 2023 after an eight-year absence. Here my network of riding buddies is much smaller. Without a group to ride with on the regular, my motorcycle has spent too much time collecting dust in my already overstuffed one-car garage. Skewing shy by nature, I’ve struggled to make friends with similar interests, infrastructure and calendars. So, on a recent weekend I did something I thought I’d never do; I met up with a Facebook group for a planned ride. I’ve been lurking on GS Riders of New Mexico for more than a year now, always finding excuses not to show up and ride along. But when member Gary Talda announced he’d be leading a ride into the Valles Caldera backcountry, I couldn’t find a reason not to go. On a chilly October Saturday morning I made my way to the designated meeting point — the Home Depot parking lot on U.S. Route 550 in Rio Rancho — rolling gracefully up to the line of motorcycles already assembled. I promptly stalled my bike to a lurching halt. On the bright side, I remembered to put my kickstand down before I dismounted. I walked up to the group of six other riders and introduced myself. I was immediately aware that in almost every case, we all were meeting each other for the first time. Talda had us circle up for a quick briefing. He reviewed the route we’d be taking — U.S. Route 550 to N.M. State Road 4 (NM 4) all the way to the entrance of the Valles Caldera National Preserve. Talda warned us that he’d be setting his cruise control at the speed limit, and if anyone was feeling spicy, they should not hesitate to pass him; we would all meet at the visitor center at Valles Caldera. Otherwise, we were advised to ride in a staggered formation and maintain a safe distance between bikes. Tom Peterson, an active member of GS Riders of NM and a very experienced rider, would tail behind as the “sweeper” to make sure none of us lambs went astray. It’s typical to have the strongest rider in a group play this role. I was second to last in the chain. I chose not to read into that. It was a spectacular October morning with cloudless, deep blue skies and temperatures hovering in the upper 50s as we rolled north. I realized quickly that I was a little under layered for the weather, but the sunshine and my heated grips were enough to stave off hypothermia. Riding or even driving up N.M. 4 is usually a treat, and today was no exception. The wide canyon from San Ysidro gradually narrows as the road winds and climbs along the Jemez River through Jemez Pueblo and Jemez Springs, with deep red rocks all around and soaring canyon walls framing the valley. The previous week’s heavy rain had left dried red mud across many stretches of the road, and I spotted an occasional boulder that had come to rest on the shoulder, suggesting the rains had been significant. But there were no road hazards of note. When our group reached the north end of Jemez Springs, we were stuck behind a volunteer police officer who kept us honest all the way to the intersection of N.M. 4 and New Mexico Road 126 (N.M. 126) in La Cueva. Given the fairly heavy traffic and brisk air temperatures, I was happy to not be racing around the tight corners. The slower pace allowed more time and attention span to take in the scenery and kept the wind chill at bay. We reached the Valles Caldera National Preserve Visitor Center around 10:30 a.m. The sun had marched higher in the sky, but its warming effects were mitigated by our much higher altitude. The digital thermometer on my instrument cluster told me it was 57 degrees, but often it reads higher because of the waste heat from the engine. It felt closer to 50 to me. Two riders, Levi from Carlsbad and Damond from Bosque Farms, were waiting for us as we pulled into the heavily graveled parking area, where my front wheel washed out and I very nearly dropped my 585-pound machine. That would prove to be the most technically challenging terrain of the entire ride. We were now nine motorcycles strong as we marched into the visitor center and descended on the park ranger, who quickly organized us. Half of our number sported annual America the Beautiful passes that admitted two people, meaning the other half of us were able to piggyback for free and avoid the $20 daily admission fee. All of us had secured a $2 backcountry permit online prior to the ride (only 40 per day are issued, so it’s best to reserve in advance at Recreation.gov), and once we proved this, the ranger gave us each a numeric code that would allow us to open the gate into the backcountry. A quick potty break and then we all mounted up and made our way to the backcountry entrance. Rolling through the gate, I realized that this was as deep into the Valles Caldera as I had ever ventured despite many visits to the preserve over the years. My expectations were high, and I was not disappointed. We followed the well-maintained gravel road for about 10 miles, surrounded by the vast, grassy meadows of the caldera interrupted here and there by forested bluffs. An occasional pothole, a couple of mud puddles, and stretches of mild washboard surfaces were all the obstacles we encountered. I’d have been very comfortable driving a standard passenger car on this road in these conditions. While the riding itself was tame, the scenery was enough to get my adrenaline flowing. I knew in my head that the caldera was some 14 miles across and almost 90,000 acres, but the scale can’t be captured by the numbers. Only by traversing this expanse did I fully appreciate just how massive an eruption it must have been to create it 1.2 million years ago. We came to a T-intersection and turned right — almost due east — following this leg about eight miles to its end near the headwaters of San Antonio Creek, which flows west to join the Jemez River before making its way to the Rio Grande. We passed a large group of folks sporting fly fishing rods who appeared to be part of a clinic. Though the creek is narrow enough to jump across in most places, it is home to a healthy population of brown trout and is a popular destination for anglers willing to make the trek. We turned around and backtracked to the T-intersection, then proceeded west for a few miles to the road’s terminus. Here we dismounted and ate what provisions we had brought. We milled about for a bit, chatting and getting to know one another a little better. Most of us were of the gray-haired variety, but there were younger, fitter riders represented as well. Except for Levi, who had ridden up from his home in Carlsbad a few days earlier to camp and explore the general area, all of us called the Albuquerque Metropolitan Area home. This happened to be the opening day of the Albuquerque International Balloon Fiesta, an event we all support but which also makes motorcyclists more than a little uncomfortable. Even without balloon-bewildered drivers, a motorcycle frequently goes unnoticed on the highway, too often with tragic results. In an average year, about 50 riders are killed in New Mexico, and about twice that number are seriously injured. Distracted driving surely is a factor in many cases, as are alcohol and unsafe riding practices. I simply refuse to ride into Albuquerque during Balloon Fiesta, and for the rest of the year I avoid riding in town as much as possible. Today’s ride was as safe as they come thanks to the remote location, perfect weather, and the fact that all of our group were equipped with full safety gear and competent riding skills. Talda called us back into a circle as we prepared to depart. He invited us to follow him as he backtracked our route via N.M. 4 and U.S. 550. Alternatively, Peterson would lead a group on a more circuitous route up N.M. 126, then south on the unpaved Forest Service Road 376 to Gilman Tunnels before reconnecting with N.M. 4 near Jemez Pueblo. A third group would venture south on Forrest Service Road 10 into Ponderosa, also rejoining N.M. 4 near Jemez Pueblo. Having ridden both routes before and feeling a bit stiff in my aging lower back from the 100 or so miles I’d already logged today, I opted to stay on the paved roads. I stopped at a gas station near the Walatowa Visitor Center to top off my now half-empty gas tank. I winced at the price of just three gallons of premium fuel. In sixth gear cruising down the highway, I can nurse about 50 miles per gallon, but on the twisty, hilly roads of the Jemez Mountains and high-revving backcountry route through the preserve, I guessed I was averaging closer to 25 miles per gallon. I’m a cheap man by nature; this fool and his money do not like to part ways. But while my fuel efficiency may have taken a hit on this ride, the smiles per gallon came at a nominal cost. If you’re riding a motorcycle in the Jemez Mountains in October with a good bunch of people, you are likely having a good day. I’m resolved to be a regular tag-along with the GS Riders of New Mexico. title: BMW Announces US Pricing And More Details On The 2027 F 450 GS - ADV Pulse
content:
BMW has released new details for the 2027 F 450 GS, adding fresh technical information and finalizing trim‑level equipment for the U.S. market. Last year, we announced the global reveal of BMW’s new lightweight parallel‑twin platform — a major step forward from the outgoing G 310 GS — and the core specifications remain unchanged. What BMW provides now is a deeper look at the engineering behind the chassis, controls, and exhaust system, along with clearer confirmation of how the bike will be packaged for U.S. buyers. With the F 450 GS positioned as BMW’s new entry point into the GS lineup, riders have been eager to see how the compact twin stacks up in an increasingly competitive segment. The latest release fills in several gaps from the original announcement but before diving into those updates, it’s worth revisiting what this new small‑displacement adventure bike brings to the category. The F 450 GS is powered by a 420cc liquid‑cooled parallel twin producing 48 hp at 8,750 rpm and 32 lb‑ft of torque at 6,750 rpm. BMW designed the compact twin around a 135‑degree crankshaft to enhance traction feel and deliver a more characterful exhaust note, pairing it with a 13.0:1 compression ratio and electronic fuel injection. Power runs through a 6‑speed transmission, and riders choosing the Sport or GS Trophy trims also receive Gear Shift Assist Pro for clutchless upshifts and downshifts. BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch (ERC), standard on the GS Trophy and optional elsewhere, automatically modulates clutch engagement to prevent stalling while preserving full engine braking, yet can be overridden manually when the rider wants full control. From there, the bike’s chassis builds on a tubular steel frame with the engine acting as a stressed member to increase rigidity and reduce overall weight. The Sport Suspension on the GS Trophy model is handled by a KYB 43mm rebound- and compression-adjustable USD fork offering 7.1 inches of travel, working in tandem with a KYB WAD rear shock that provides spring preload and rebound adjustment along with travel‑dependent damping. A hollow‑cast aluminum swingarm helps reduce unsprung weight, and tubeless cross‑spoked wheels come standard on the GS Trophy variant. Ergonomics follow a neutral riding triangle designed for both seated and standing control, supported by seat height options of 32.7, 33.3, and 34.0 inches. BMW includes adjustable brake and clutch levers, as well as adjustable gearshift and footbrake levers, giving riders more flexibility to tailor the cockpit for off‑road use. Rounding out the package is a full suite of electronics that includes Rain, Road, and Enduro riding modes, with Enduro Pro reserved for the Sport and GS Trophy. ABS Pro, Dynamic Traction Control (DTC), Engine Drag Torque Control (MSR), and Dynamic Brake Control (DBC) provide additional support, while a 6.5‑inch TFT display with smartphone connectivity comes standard along with full LED lighting and a USB‑C charging port. BMW claims a top speed of 102 mph and 0–62 mph in 5.9 seconds, giving the F 450 GS respectable highway performance for a small‑bore adventure bike while still maintaining the compact footprint needed for off‑road maneuverability. BMW’s latest announcement provides a clearer picture of the bike’s component design and adjustability. The Bavarian manufacturer now specifies that the new alloy wheels on the base model are 2.2 lbs lighter than those on the G 310 GS, reducing unsprung weight and improving responsiveness. They also confirm that both the gearshift and footbrake levers are adjustable, along with the brake and clutch hand levers, giving riders more flexibility in tailoring the cockpit for off‑road use. Additional clarity was provided on the exhaust system, which uses a stainless‑steel design with two catalytic converters, and on the rear suspension, which employs a KYB central spring strut with preload and rebound adjustment and travel‑dependent damping (WAD). BMW also notes that the hollow‑cast aluminum swingarm contributes to both weight savings and rigidity. Cross‑spoked wheels, standard on the GS Trophy, will be available as an option on other trims beginning with July 2027 production. Finally, BMW has provided a more detailed explanation of how their Easy Ride Clutch system works. Previously described only as an anti‑stall feature, they now explain that the system automatically adds a small amount of clutch slip whenever engine speed drops too low, helping prevent stalls during slow, technical maneuvers or abrupt downshifts. At the same time, it keeps enough mechanical connection to maintain a natural engine‑braking feel, rather than disengaging the clutch completely. BMW also clarified that ERC is fully overrideable: the moment the rider uses the clutch lever deliberately, the system steps aside. BMW states the F 450 GS will reach U.S. dealers in Q1 2027, finalizing the rollout window previously estimated between late 2026 and early 2027. title: A Little Hell-Raiser: We Drive the 1992 Mazda MX-3 GS - Car and Driver
content: A car that winks at you. And then sings and dances too. “Mazda will make vehicles that wink at you,” proclaimed chairman Kenichi Yamamoto. As mission statements go, that’s a catchy line. The MX-3 has an air about it. Sitting there, looking quirky and racy and maybe even a little frivolous, it kind of grins a conspiratorial grin. It chucks you under the chin with a promise of fun times to come. “Hey, you’re not doing anything. Whaddya say we go raise a little hell?” A car that winks at you? When it appears this fall, the MX-3 will run in the small sports-specialty category, a class bursting at its little seams with such sporty coupes as the new Toyota Pa­seo and Nissan NX, plus the familiar Isuzu Impulse/Geo Storm and Honda CRX. (The CRX is the lone two-plus­-none among a pack of two-plus-twos.) Mazda hopes, however, that you’ll view the MX-3 a little differently. Not so much as another zippy two-plus-two coupe based on cheap-sedan hardware, but rath­er as a sports car with distinction. Two distinctions, actually: real four-passenger capacity, and the automotive world’s smallest V-6 engine. See all results for used 1992 Mazda MX-3 for sale near 85032 We wonder just how “real” that occu­pancy rate is, but there’s no denying that this high-revving, four-cam 1845 cc six in­troduces a new class of powerplant, bring­ing to the small-coupe segment the silky snarl that comes only from sixes. (Mazda is also looking to steal thunder from Volkswagen, which after many years of struggle is just now readying its narrow-­angle V-6 for production in the Corrado.) Catchy styling makes the right first im­pression, combining rounded forms, a wedgy profile, a sharply raked windshield (65 degrees from vertical), and a vast, wrap-over rear window. It looks sharp, and heads swivel all around the MX-3 on the road. Aero add-ons help trim the Cd to 0.31. Notable aesthetic details include the curvature at the rear edge of the side win­dows and a tiny glass panel beneath the rear spoiler, in the batch’s vertical face. The latter is touted as an aid to visibility but seems so shallow as to be more useful as a styling element, to keep the tail from looking too thick and flat. Wheelbase (96.3 inches) and front and rear track (57.5 and 57.7 inches) are very generous for this class, giving the MX-3 a big footprint—which is a promising start for good handling—as well as a surpris­ingly roomy cabin. From the driver’s po­sition, the interior looks wide, open, and spacious. It also looks attractive and well laid out, though much less distinctively contoured than the sheetmetal. The front seats easily accommodate large adults without crowding, and they offer good side bolstering that stops short of impeding entry and exit. And what of that back seat, which Mazda claims is not a “plus-two” penalty box, but a place where average-size people can ride “in reasonable posture”? It is quite wide (and attractive, with a continuous, wrap­around effect at back and sides but clearly defined bun pockets), but an occupant’s head, knees, and feet need to be located precisely where Mazda intended in order to find a fit. It is possible to carry two adults back there, but they should be good sports—literally, because it’s an athletic clamber into place—and the trip shouldn’t be much farther than down to the video store. See all results for used 1992 Mazda MX-3 for sale near 85032 Most of the car’s sloping front end is over the horizon from the driver’s eye, a minor packaging miracle considering the giant lump of engine the hood has to cov­er. Though 1.8 liters is hardly a lot of swept volume, it takes a load of far-flung aluminum to enclose it and its valve gear and manifolding in a V configuration. One glance at the outbreak of cam covers and intake runners under the MX-3’s hood shows why orthodoxy for these effi­ciency-minded coupes is four cylinders in a neat little row. But it all fits, and an impressive collec­tion of machinery it is. The transversely mounted V-6’s main castings are all-alu­minum, with the cylinder banks angled at 60 degrees. Twin camshafts in each cylinder head operate four valves per cylinder, whose breathing efficiency is aided by an intake tract that uses two solenoid-controlled butterfly valves to vary its effective volume and fatten the torque curve. Mazda engineers correctly anticipated that low- and mid-range torque was going to need help in this short-stroke, high-­rpm engine, and some drivers are sure to wonder if it got enough. The SAE net out­put ratings are 130 horsepower at 6500 rpm and 115 pound-feet of torque at 4500 (numbers that meet or beat those of every car in the class except the NX2000’s 140 hp and 130 pound-feet). But on the go, the free-spinning little six often seems to gen­erate the sensations of speed more effec­tively than it does real thrust. Around 3000 rpm, the exhaust reso­nates with a gorgeous snarl that evokes the E-type Jaguar 3.8, yet there’s little power to be had down there. Not until 4500 does the small of your back start to register acceleration, and then only in the lower gears. Rapid progress demands lots of revs, like in the range from 5000 to the 7000-rpm redline. That can feel a trifle overdramatic in traffic, but at least the en­gine is happy to do it. It’s marvelously smooth and responsive, though up there, the Jaguar snarl is replaced by a muted whir that recalls Mazda’s rotary engine. A light-action, rod-linkage gearbox provides smooth if slightly long throws for stirring through the five ratios. The five-speed’s gear spacing is probably as good as it can be, but the one-two gap is pretty broad. Peg the tach in first (33 mph at 7000 rpm) and the shift to second drops revs all the way to about 3900—a bit be­low the fringe of torque territory. As soon as we can mate a production MX-3 to our instruments, we—and you—will know a lot more about how the impressions from this pre-production example translate into hard performance data. Fortunately, a well-sorted chassis con­tributes to the MX-3’s back-road fun fac­tor. And, for that matter, to its freeway composure. This is the company, remem­ber, that coined the term “stagility,” de­noting a combination of stability and agil­ity. And the firm strut-type suspension, a refinement of the system used by the Pro­tege and Escort/Tracer sedans, does in fact give fine directional stability along with quick cornering response. Engine­-speed-sensitive power steering feels light and quick, and the dartiness we’ve no­ticed before in this rear-suspension design is much better controlled. There will actually be two MX-3s. The one we’ve been talking about is tagged the GS. There’s also a base model, but its 88-horsepower, SOHC 1.6-liter four, leaves it out of the real news. Differences include a disc/drum brake arrangement in place of the GS’s four-wheel discs, smaller tires (185/65 versus 205/55) on fourteen-inch steel wheels rather than the fifteen-inch alloys fitted to the GS, and a slower steer­ing ratio (17:1 compared with 15:1). An electronically controlled four-speed auto­matic can replace the manual box in ei­ther model, though we can’t imagine who would opt for it, especially with the playful, torqueless six. Prices have not yet been announced, but they will have to be competitive among small sporty coupes, meaning suggested retails in the low teens. The smooth and slinky MX-3 will shortly take its place among the RX-7, the Miata, and the MPV as the sort of specialized, off-center vehicle on which Mazda is building a name. If Mr. Yamamoto has his way, it will not only wink at you, but will also grab your sleeve and drag you off, promising an experience just a little different from what you’ve had with ev­erything else out there. 1992 Mazda MX-3 GSVehicle Type: front-engine, front-wheel-drive, 2+2-passenger, 2-door coupe ENGINEDOHC 24-valve V-6, aluminum block and heads, port fuel injectionDisplacement: 113 in3, 1845 cm3Power: 130 bhp @ 6500 rpmTorque: 115 lb-ft @ 4500 rpm CHASSISSuspension, F/R: struts/multilinkBrakes, F/R: 10.1-in vented disc/9.8-in discTire Size: P205/55VR-15 DIMENSIONSWheelbase: 96.3 inLength: 165.7 inWidth: 66.7 inHeight: 51.6 inPassenger Volume, F/R: 49/30 ft3Cargo Volume: 15 ft3Curb Weight: 2550 lb C/D PERFORMANCE ESTIMATES60 mph: 8.5 sec1/4-Mile: 16.0 sec @ 85 mphTop Speed: 125 mph Front-Wheel-Drive Heresy? The near term swing factor is the upcoming earnings report, where investors want to see that higher non compensation expenses and softer fixed income trading are not eroding return on equity. The main operational risk right now sits in that mix of higher costs and weaker FICC activity, set against a balance sheet that relies entirely on higher risk funding sources rather than customer deposits. The recent run of new fixed rate notes, much of it callable and medium term, looks more like regular funding than a game changer for the equity story. The more important test is still quarterly profitability and capital flexibility. The most relevant recent development for this funding spree is the series of US dollar and peso fixed income offerings, including the 6.40% Notes due April 19, 2035 and the zero coupon Euro MTN in Mexican pesos. This cluster of callable medium term notes extends across maturities from 2027 out to 2051, with several senior and unsecured tranches at par pricing. Execution risk arises if higher funding costs and heavier balance sheet usage compress returns just as non compensation expenses step up. That would test the thesis that technology and a richer advisory and asset management mix can support firm wide margins.
